section_title: When should love change how someone uses freedom?

versions.label: BSB
paragraphs: 7 But not everyone has this knowledge. Some people are still so accustomed to idols that they eat such food as if it were sacrificed to an idol. And since their conscience is weak, it is defiled. 8 But food does not bring us closer to God: We are no worse if we do not eat, and no better if we do. 9 Be careful, however, that your freedom does not become a stumbling block to the weak.

10 For if someone with a weak conscience sees you who are well informed eating in an idol’s temple, will he not be encouraged to eat food sacrificed to idols? 11 So this weak brother, for whom Christ died, is destroyed by your knowledge. 12 By sinning against your brothers in this way and wounding their weak conscience, you sin against Christ. 13 Therefore, if what I eat causes my brother to stumble, I will never eat meat again, so that I will not cause him to stumble.

context_lines: Not everyone has left old associations with idols behind in the same way. Some eat the food as though still participating in its worship, and their conscience is wounded. Paul says food itself does not bring someone closer to God, but the effect on another person still matters.

He pictures a believer seen eating in an idol’s temple. Archaeologists have found dining rooms and cooking facilities at Corinth’s sanctuary of Demeter and Kore; see the [excavation summary](https://www.ascsa.edu.gr/publications/book/?i=9780876611838). This illustrates the connection between sanctuaries and meals without identifying that sanctuary as the place Paul means.

The danger is that a person with a troubled conscience may follow the example into conduct he still understands as involvement with idols. This is more than someone disliking another person’s food choice. Paul treats leading a brother into sin as an offense against that brother and against Christ, who died for him.

Paul would therefore give up meat rather than cause that harm. The discussion continues through chapter 10, where [1 Corinthians 10:14–22](https://biblehub.com/bsb/1_corinthians/10.htm) explicitly forbids participation in idolatry. Concern for conscience is not a declaration that joining pagan worship becomes harmless whenever someone feels free to do it.
common_interpretation_lines: Christians commonly recognize the call to put a brother or sister’s good above the enjoyment of a freedom. The warning about the brother being destroyed is taken seriously, though traditions differ over whether someone truly brought into grace can finally be lost.

[Wesley’s note on verse 11](https://wesley.nnu.edu/john-wesley/john-wesleys-notes-on-the-bible/notes-on-st-pauls-first-epistle-to-the-corinthians/) reads it as a real possibility that someone for whom Christ died may perish. The [Methodist Articles, Article XII](https://www.umc.org/en/content/articles-of-religion), likewise allow departure from grace and restoration through God’s grace. Catholic [Catechism 1857–1861](https://www.vatican.va/content/catechism/en/part_three/section_one/chapter_one/article_8/iv_the_gravity_of_sin_mortal_and_venial_sin.html) teaches that grave sin committed with full knowledge and deliberate consent can bring loss of God’s saving grace, with repentance and God’s forgiveness necessary for restoration.

The Reformed [Westminster Confession 17.1–3](https://www.opc.org/wcf.html) instead affirms that those God truly accepts in Christ will not finally fall away, even though they can fall into serious sin. These broader differences affect how readers understand the warning’s final outcome; they do not remove Paul’s demand to avoid harming a fellow believer.
god_plan_lines: A useful parallel appears in [Matthew 18:10–14](https://biblehub.com/bsb/matthew/18.htm), where Jesus describes a shepherd seeking one sheep that has wandered and the Father’s concern that His little ones should not perish. The point of comparison is care for the person in danger, rather than an assumption that every detail names exactly the same situation.

Paul’s reminder that Christ died for the weak brother gives that care its weight here. The person affected by a meal is someone Christ has loved at great cost. In God’s purpose of gathering and caring for His people, that person’s good matters more than another believer’s opportunity to demonstrate freedom.
